n: Job answers Bildad. This chapter moves from the depths of despair to one of the greatest declarations of faith in all scripture.
Job asks how long his friends will keep tormenting him and crushing him with words.
“Ten times” means “over and over.” Job says they are not ashamed to treat him so harshly.

f.g: Wrong me, treat me harshly (the Hebrew is uncertain).

n: Even if Job has made some mistake, it is his own concern — it hasn’t harmed them, and they have no right to condemn him for it.
If the friends insist on lifting themselves above him and using his disgrace as evidence against him…

f.g: My humiliation — his suffering, which they treat as proof of guilt.

n: …then they should know that it is God who has thrown him down, not his own sin. Job answers Bildad’s trap imagery (18:8-10): the net is God’s.
Job cries “Violence!” but no one hears; he calls for help but finds no justice.

f.g: Literally “I cry, ‘Violence!’” — the call of someone being attacked.

n: God has walled off his road and covered his path in darkness — Job feels trapped with no way forward.
Job has been stripped of his honor and the crown of his reputation.

f.w: taken the crown from my head

n: He feels torn down on every side, his hope uprooted like a tree — a sad reversal of his earlier hope for a tree that sprouts again (14:7).
Job feels God’s anger burning against him, as though God counts him an enemy.
He pictures God’s troops building siege ramps and camping around his tent — overwhelming force against one small man.
Now Job lists the people who have abandoned him, starting with his brothers and acquaintances.

f.w: put my brethren far from me

n: His relatives and closest friends have failed him and forgotten him.

f.g: Intimate friends, those who knew him well.

n: Even guests and servant girls in his house treat him like a foreigner.
He calls his own servant and gets no answer, even when he begs.
His wife finds his breath repulsive, and his own brothers are disgusted by him.

f.w: the children's sake of mine own body
f.g: Probably “my own brothers” (sons of my mother’s womb), since Job’s children have died.

n: Even little children make fun of him; when he gets up, they mock.
His closest friends now loathe him, and those he loved have turned against him.
He is skin and bones and has escaped death only by the narrowest margin — the origin of the phrase “by the skin of my teeth.”

f.g: A barely-there margin; the expression in English comes from this verse.

n: Job begs his friends for pity, since God’s hand has struck him. It is a raw, human plea for kindness.

f.w: the hand of God hath touched me

n: Why do they hound him as God seems to? Aren’t they satisfied with tearing at his flesh?

f.g: An idiom for slander — “eating someone’s flesh.”

n: Job longs for his words to be written down as a lasting record, so that future generations will know his testimony.
Better still, carved into rock with an iron chisel and filled with lead so they could never be erased.

f.g: An engraving tool and lead poured into carved letters to make them stand out.

n: The heart of the book: Job knows his Redeemer lives and will stand on the earth at the last day. Latter-day Saints see this as a testimony of Jesus Christ, the living Redeemer.

f.g: Hebrew go’el — a kinsman who rescues, avenges, or buys back a family member.

f.w: he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth

n: Even after his body decays, Job declares, in his flesh he will see God. Latter-day Saints read this as a clear witness of a literal, physical resurrection.

f.w: in my flesh shall I see God

n: Job will see God with his own eyes, personally, not through someone else — and his heart longs for that day.

f.g: Kidneys; the innermost self — “my heart faints with longing.”

n: Job warns the friends: if they keep saying the root of his trouble lies in him, they are wrong.
He warns them to fear God’s judgment themselves, for their false accusations deserve it. In the end God does rebuke them (42:7).
